endorsements.quote: Therefore, when developing chatbots, it is important to determine whether they are classified as medical devices and, if so, which risk class they fall under.
Data privacy and security, while not in the scope of this paper , must always comply with national or regional rules, such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) in Europe [29].
Regular audits and stress tests should be conducted to ensure compliance with security standards.
Regular updates should be applied to comply with the latest security standards to protect users, along with a clear incident response plan in case of a breach.
Medicine and healthcare could benefit from chatbots if their scope is carefully defined and if they are used appropriately and monitored long-term.
One way to mitigate these risks is by restricting chatbots to a specific knowledge base through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).
Finally , if the device is decommissioned, specific rules for ending its active use must also be followed.

unlisted_practices: Implement a quality management system and adhere to relevant ISO standards even for chatbots not classified as medical devices.
Add control layers that fall back to no response when a chatbot is asked about topics outside its scope.
Have a designated chatbot master regularly review prompts and answers for accuracy and harmlessness.
Review recurring user prompts not yet covered by the knowledge base as part of ongoing quality improvement.
Complete verification and validation and provide user training before deploying a chatbot.

screen.reason: The paper is a perspective/regulatory framework article using a single chatbot as a case study to outline certification processes and regulatory compliance under Swiss law and the EU AI Act.
